title: Can AI Change How We Deal with Disasters?
gist: A RAND study for the Markle Foundation's AIDE initiative mapped 1,179 AI-enabled products already usable by emergency management — far more than expected — and concludes the binding constraint is not technology supply but market opacity (no clearinghouse, unknowable pricing, no cyber attestations) and organizational capacity to integrate, govern, and sustain tools. Supply skews heavily to response over preparedness and long-term recovery, and without stronger diffusion mechanisms the authors expect little near-term adoption progress.

themes.theme: Unexpected supply glut of AI tools

insights.claim: A RAND market scan identified 1,179 AI-enabled products already available that could support emergency management, versus the research team's going-in assumption of maybe dozens.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: The emergency-management AI market is far more crowded than assumed — new entrants face immediate competitive density, and the scarce asset is distribution and integration, not model capability.
insights.quote: how do you collect systematic, consistent information along a lot of different dimensions about 1,179 products?
insights.locator: Then, because we always had that second interest

insights.claim: A nationwide Argonne National Laboratory study whose results were released in 2025 found emergency management at the very nascent stages of technology adoption, with very few agencies accessing or using AI-enabled products.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Establishes a near-zero installed base as of 2025 — the addressable greenfield is large but the historical adoption rate is the base case for forecasting.
insights.quote: That available information in 2025 suggested that emergency management is at its very nascent stages, with very, very few having access to or using AI-enabled products.
insights.locator: So we have both authoritative evidence and anecdotal evidence.

insights.claim: Anecdotal evidence a year after the Argonne baseline shows emergency managers actively experimenting with general-purpose LLMs such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini within whatever boundaries their organizations allow.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Horizontal LLM vendors are getting bottom-up penetration into public-safety workflows ahead of any vertical procurement cycle — a wedge that specialized vendors must displace.
insights.quote: LLMs for sure are getting a lot of attention.
insights.locator: That said, a year later, the landscape of AI

insights.claim: Many emergency management organizations already run AI without labeling it as such — forecasting, mapping, imagery analysis, translation, and information monitoring all embed AI components.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Survey-based 'AI adoption' figures for the public sector understate real penetration; embedded AI in incumbent GIS and weather platforms is the true competitive baseline.
insights.quote: For example, forecasting, mapping, imagery analysis, translation, information monitoring are all using elements of AI-enabled tools, but they may not know that they are actually embedded in those tools that they already using.
insights.locator: As Jessica said, the adoption is uneven

insights.claim: The core problem in this market is not an absence of technology but the difficulty of seeing the market clearly and judging what is credible, relevant, and sustainable.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Reframes the opportunity from building tools to building trust infrastructure — evaluation, certification, and curation layers capture value where product supply is already abundant.
insights.quote: it's less an issue of the absence of technology than the difficulty of seeing the market clearly and knowing what is credible, relevant, and sustainable
insights.locator: Maybe not so much the specific tools

insights.claim: AI product supply is heavily skewed toward the response phase of emergency management, with fewer tools for recovery and many fewer for preparedness.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Preparedness and long-term recovery are the structurally underserved segments — the whitespace for a new entrant that wants to avoid the crowded response market.
insights.quote: There are a lot more products out there that support the response phase, fewer for recovery, and many, many fewer for the preparedness phase.
insights.locator: Sure, and as Jessica and you emphasized

insights.claim: Within the response phase, the most crowded product categories are situational awareness, hazard monitoring, and information sharing — tools fusing satellite imagery, drones, cameras, sensors, weather data, news, and social media.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Highest competitive density and likely price compression sits in situational-awareness fusion; differentiation there requires integration depth rather than new data sources.
insights.quote: So the most crowded area within response was situational awareness, hazard monitoring, and information sharing.
insights.locator: But we also discovered they're not evenly distributed

insights.claim: Documented coverage gaps include fatality management, emergency debris and route clearance, family reunification, natural and cultural resource restoration, public-private sector coordination, land use, rebuilding, and mitigation planning.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: A concrete, published list of unserved workflows — effectively a product roadmap for anyone building into government disaster budgets.
insights.quote: So for example, some of them within the response phase would be those that serve fatality management services, emergency debris clearance and route clearance, family reunification, those types of things.
insights.locator: We actually have an entire appendix on the gaps

insights.claim: The market's orientation toward response and organizational needs leaves preparedness, long-term recovery, and the survivor experience underbuilt, which the authors frame as an explicit opening for the technology sector.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: A named invitation from a RAND study commissioned by a funder — the kind of signal that precedes grant-funded pilots and philanthropic capital flowing to survivor-facing tools.
insights.quote: And frankly, gaps actually create opportunities, especially for the technology sector, to step into where those gaps are and help fulfill those needs.
insights.locator: I was also struck by the imbalance

themes.theme: The stacking problem and product-level friction

insights.claim: Available tools are very narrow — each delivers a slice of insight without connecting the separate data streams or synthesizing them into decision-ready insight.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Point solutions cannot win the situational-awareness budget; the platform that fuses and synthesizes streams is where consolidation value accrues.
insights.quote: So each one's doing this very narrow little slice—and not only does it not connect the data, put it all in one place—but it also doesn't synthesize it
insights.locator: I think a big, huge challenge

insights.claim: Narrow tooling forces a 'stacking problem' in which agencies must buy, connect, and maintain many separate products, each demanding different operator skill levels — compounding purchase and maintenance cost.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for any low-capacity public-sector buyer: fragmentation, not license price, is the real cost driver — and the argument for suite-level bundling.
insights.quote: So people would have to have a whole bunch of these and connect them.
insights.locator: And so we call that

insights.claim: Most products on the market require IT expertise for onboarding and ongoing use, which many emergency management organizations simply do not have on staff.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Implementation services and managed offerings are a required attach for this buyer; self-serve SaaS motions will stall.
insights.quote: most of the products on the market require technical expertise, someone who knows IT, right?
insights.locator: So, getting into just a couple of specific examples

insights.claim: Nearly all products require a consistent internet connection, which is a manageable constraint for day-to-day preparedness use but a severe limitation for response, when connectivity is most likely to fail.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Offline and edge-capable architectures are a genuine differentiator in disaster response — a rare technical moat in a crowded field.
insights.quote: Additionally, most of the products, nearly all require internet connection—consistent internet connection—to use.
insights.locator: Additionally, most of the products

insights.claim: A significant proportion of products require a separate base platform to function at all, so buyers wanting only add-on functionality must also purchase the underlying platform.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Platform lock-in is already structural in this market; incumbent base-platform vendors capture the add-on economics of the AI wave.
insights.quote: we discovered a lot of the products on the market require another product to even function
insights.locator: And compounding this issue of not being able to tell how much things cost

insights.claim: RAND, with large teams and AI-assisted collection, found it impossible to determine reliable pricing for these products — pricing opacity is near-universal in the segment.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: If a research institution cannot price the market, budget-constrained agencies cannot plan purchases; published pricing is an immediate, cheap competitive differentiator for a vendor.
insights.quote: We saw on the market that finding out what the price was of these things was impossible.
insights.locator: We saw on the market that finding out what the price was

insights.claim: Most products carry an evident privacy concern involving personally identifiable or jurisdictional information, while many vendors publish no outward-facing evidence of cyber certification of any kind.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Security attestations (FedRAMP-style certification, published audits) are an unmet buyer requirement — a gating factor that will separate winners as procurement matures.
insights.quote: a lot of the companies out on the market don't provide outward facing evidence of cyber certification of any kind
insights.locator: So, again, as Glen was saying

themes.theme: Adoption capacity as the real bottleneck

insights.claim: The biggest barrier to AI in emergency management is not product availability but organizational capacity to evaluate, acquire, integrate, govern, and sustain a product after the initial demonstration.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Pilot-to-production conversion — not pilot count — is the metric that matters for any vendor selling into this sector; demo wins are not revenue.
insights.quote: the biggest barrier may not be product availability
insights.locator: Sure, some of the things we found was that

insights.claim: Demand on emergency management is growing faster than capacity, with the field chronically under-resourced at state, local, tribal, and territorial levels and the gap widening.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Structural under-resourcing caps willingness to pay regardless of product value — the market expands only if budget policy changes, not because need rises.
insights.quote: demand on emergency management is growing faster than capacity is
insights.locator: Sure. Let's start off with the basic problem.

insights.claim: Disaster events increasingly overlap and cascade, so a single wildfire simultaneously becomes an evacuation, public health, housing, utility, economic, and recovery problem.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Cascade dynamics mean tools scoped to a single hazard type systematically under-serve the actual operating picture — argues for cross-domain data models.
insights.quote: For example, a wildfire can become an evacuation, a public health, a housing, a utility, and economic and recovery problem all at the same time.
insights.locator: Events are also increasingly overlapping

insights.claim: Larger, better-resourced agencies will adopt AI tools sooner while smaller jurisdictions risk being left behind absent shared support structures, producing a two-tier capability landscape.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Expect early revenue concentration in a handful of large metros and states; shared-services or cooperative purchasing models are the only path to the long tail.
insights.quote: larger and better resourced organizations may be able to adopt sooner, while smaller jurisdictions risk being left behind unless there's some type of shared support
insights.locator: So, the issues are manageable one at a time

insights.claim: Emergency managers are professionally trained risk managers, which makes them structurally risk-averse buyers who must clear governance, data, and integration reviews before full adoption.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Sales cycles into this buyer will be long and evidence-driven; models projecting fast SaaS-style adoption curves are likely wrong.
insights.quote: Emergency managers, I mean, their job is risk management, which tends to also make them a bit risk averse.
insights.locator: Emergency managers, I mean, their job is risk management

insights.claim: RAND proposes an organizational readiness assessment across applicability, adoptability, adaptability, integration and dependencies, reliability, governance and risk, and procurement and resources.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: A concrete checklist likely to become the de facto evaluation rubric in this sector — vendors should pre-answer all seven dimensions in their collateral.
insights.quote: we need to assess organizational readiness in an emergency management organization across several areas: applicability, adoptability, adaptability, integration and dependencies, reliability, governance and risk, procurement and resources
insights.locator: For emergency managers, I would start with the mission problem

insights.claim: The recommended buying discipline is to start with the mission problem rather than the technology, and to define in advance how the tool's contribution will be evaluated.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Mission-first framing predicts which vendors win: those who lead with a specific operational task, not model capability claims.
insights.quote: I would start with the mission problem, not with the technology.
insights.locator: Well, let's separate emergency managers and policymakers

insights.claim: There is no central repository or clearinghouse of AI products for emergency management, and no standardized product information across vendor websites, making discovery a laborious word-of-mouth process.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: The missing curation layer is itself a business — and whoever builds the trusted registry gains distribution leverage over the 1,179-product supply.
insights.quote: There isn't a central repository or clearinghouse that exists for the emergency managers who are doing the work
insights.locator: So this is a really big challenge.

insights.claim: Emergency managers rely heavily on trusted peers and a small, tightly connected professional community that candidly shares what works — peer networks, not vendor claims, are the diffusion channel.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Reference selling and practitioner advocacy dominate; a single bad deployment propagates fast through a small community and can foreclose a market.
insights.quote: The emergency management community is actually fairly small.
insights.locator: Yeah, exactly. Emergency managers, as Jessica said, rely heavily on trusted peers.

insights.claim: Absent significantly stronger diffusion mechanisms across the fields involved in disaster work, the authors expect no substantial near-term progress in AI adoption despite abundant supply.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Explicitly deflates near-term revenue expectations for vendors selling into this vertical — the constraint is diffusion infrastructure, not demand or product.
insights.quote: in the near future without greater and more significant mechanisms to propel this diffusion across these fields, we can't expect to see a ton of progress in the near term
insights.locator: Now that may evolve in any number of these spaces over time

insights.claim: A credible clearinghouse, practitioner networks, independent evaluations, and shared procurement support are the specific mechanisms identified as making this market navigable.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Names four fundable intervention points — likely targets for philanthropic or federal money and therefore where early institutional capital will land.
insights.quote: So some sort of credible clearinghouse, practitioner networks, independent evaluations, maybe even shared procurement support can make the market much easier to navigate for emergency managers.
insights.locator: Yeah, exactly. Emergency managers, as Jessica said, rely heavily on trusted peers.

insights.claim: In preparedness, AI's largest payoff is displacing administrative load — grant seeking and reporting, plan writing, exercise development, training, and public outreach materials — work that agencies often pay contractors to do.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: The near-term budget being disrupted is the consulting and contractor line item, not headcount — a displacement trade rather than a new-spend trade.
insights.quote: Emergency managers spend a ton of time on those activities. Tons of time. What AI can do is alleviate the amount of time that is spent on those tasks. It can also save a lot of money.
insights.locator: Well, maybe I'll start with preparedness.

insights.claim: The clearest response-phase opportunity is faster sensemaking: pulling together multiple information streams, flagging changes or anomalies, and cutting the time staff spend manually sorting information.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Time-to-decision is the metric that justifies procurement in response; vendors should benchmark against manual sorting time, not model accuracy.
insights.quote: But the clearest opportunity from AI is faster sensemaking.
insights.locator: And I'll start with the response.

insights.claim: Computer vision can compare pre- and post-event imagery to flag likely damage and prioritize where field verification is most urgent, serving both initial response and intensive recovery damage assessment.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: A well-defined, high-value workflow with clear ROI — the most procurement-ready AI category in the disaster stack, and relevant to insurance claims adjacency.
insights.quote: So computer vision can compare pre- and post-event imagery, flag likely damage, and help teams decide where field verification is most urgent.
insights.locator: The second example would be damage assessment

insights.claim: AI's distinctive contribution to sensemaking is weak-signal detection: identifying what human operators miss because adrenaline in an emergency operations center pulls attention toward the loudest events.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: A cognitive-bias argument for AI that generalizes beyond disasters to any high-tempo operations center — trading floors, network operations, security operations.
insights.quote: you pay a lot of attention to the big noisy things, but you might be missing some of the weaker signals that will give you more information
insights.locator: Yeah, and I'll add that this idea of sensemaking

insights.claim: Fusing data sources should allow prediction of where disaster needs will be greatest, addressing the long-documented pattern that disabled people suffer more and recover more slowly than other population segments.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Equity-targeted prediction is a differentiated product angle likely to attract philanthropic and federal grant funding rather than agency operating budgets.
insights.quote: the disabled suffer more and their recoveries are longer than other segments of the population
insights.locator: If I could add, Glen, you know, it could also really help us predict

insights.claim: The stated value proposition is capacity augmentation for a limited workforce while preserving human judgment and accountability — explicitly not automation or replacement of emergency managers.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Positioning that avoids replacement backlash is a procurement prerequisite in public safety; 'autonomous decisioning' claims are a liability with this buyer.
insights.quote: The value proposition is not replacing emergency managers, it's giving a limited workforce more capacity while preserving human judgment and accountability.
insights.locator: Emergency managers are also flooded with data

insights.claim: Technology companies are advised to design for a low-capacity, low-technical-knowledge buyer, communicate in lay language, and stop hiding price — basic go-to-market changes that gate purchasability.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Transparent pricing and plain-language positioning are cheap, immediately actionable differentiators in a market where nearly no vendor does either.
insights.quote: Price is a huge issue; don't hide it.
insights.locator: Looking over on the technology company side

insights.claim: Vendors should let the mission define the requirement rather than the tool, because historically adopted technologies have created more requirements, staff time, labor, and cost instead of alleviating them.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: A veteran practitioner's prior that new tech adds net work — the default skepticism any vendor must overcome with evidence from realistic conditions.
insights.quote: I've seen many technologies that have been adopted that created more requirements that didn't serve the mission, and more staff time, and more labor, and more cost as opposed to actually alleviating any of those things.
insights.locator: And I think I'd add on for the technology companies

insights.claim: Emergency managers themselves have very little control over adoption; IT departments, procurement rule-setters, and elected officials making budget decisions hold the actual decision rights.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Sell to the control points — IT governance and procurement policy — rather than to the end user who cannot authorize a purchase.
insights.quote: Relative to policymakers and technology companies, emergency managers have very little control here.
insights.locator: Talking about policymakers for a second

insights.claim: AI governance decisions being made across the country right now will determine whether emergency management can use these tools, and it is too early to tell whether they will facilitate or block adoption.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: State-level AI governance rules are an unpriced binary risk sitting on top of every public-sector AI revenue forecast — worth tracking as a leading indicator.
insights.quote: It is too early to say whether those will facilitate emergency management's ability to avail themselves of these tools or not, but have no doubt the decisions they make are going to control what happens.
insights.locator: Also, just to put it out there, AI governance

insights.claim: The Markle Foundation, through its AI for Disasters and Emergencies (AIDE) initiative, will fund efforts to upskill the emergency management workforce on AI.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Named philanthropic capital entering AI training for a public-sector vertical — a concrete near-term funding flow for training providers and a demand catalyst.
insights.quote: the Markle Foundation will be funding some efforts to help upskill the workforce as well as the initiative moves forward
insights.locator: So a big opportunity for emergency managers is to seek professional development

insights.claim: RAND used LLM-driven code pipelines plus robust human and automated verification to collect systematic data on 1,179 products, and states the study could not have been done at scale or on schedule without AI.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: A concrete proof point that AI changes the unit economics of market-mapping research — relevant to anyone valuing research, due-diligence, or data-collection businesses.
insights.quote: But without AI, we could not have done this study at scale and in the timeframe that we had.
insights.locator: We had human verification processes that were really robust

insights.claim: The overarching takeaway is that more technology is not needed — the implementation environment is equally or more important than the existence of the tools, and disaster costs are on an unsustainable trajectory.
insights.speaker: RAND Corporation
insights.so_what: Capital deployed into more disaster-AI products faces diminishing returns; the marginal dollar earns more in integration, governance, and adoption infrastructure.
insights.quote: We cannot afford the trajectory we're on.
insights.locator: So I would add, because we're talking about an audience
